passage_changes.passage: The Houthi movement is an armed group in Yemen that has grown into one of the most powerful forces in the country's long conflict. It began as an opposition movement during the rule of Ali Abdullah Saleh, who had governed North Yemen for many years. The movement's early history is closely tied to a series of wars in Saada, a northern region, which started after the group's founder was killed by Yemeni forces. The 2011 uprising in Yemen, part of the wider Arab Spring, forced Saleh to hand over power to a new leader. The new government then faced an economic crisis and security threats from militant groups, including an al-Qaeda branch that captured territory in parts of the south and east. The Houthis used this instability to expand their territory, moving into the capital and later into western Yemen. Their growth drew a military response from Saudi Arabia, which intervened to restore the internationally recognised government. Today the Houthis remain a central actor in the Yemeni civil war, and their control over key areas shapes regional politics and maritime security along the Red Sea.

Pakistan and China have set up a Boundary Joint Commission to watch over how their border management arrangements are put into practice. The body is meant to help the two sides coordinate on the everyday business of a shared frontier, including joint surveys, the flow of trade across the boundary and ties between people on either side. Its roots lie in an earlier bilateral framework on managing the boundary, which laid the groundwork for the new institution. The arrangement has drawn a firm response from India, which maintains that the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are integral parts of the country. New Delhi has questioned the move and reaffirmed its own claims over the territory concerned. The dispute centres on the Shaksgam Valley, a mountainous stretch in the Karakoram region, which came under a boundary agreement signed in the 1960s. Routes and infrastructure that link Xinjiang with Pakistan add to the importance of the arrangement, because they strengthen connectivity in a sensitive part of the western Himalayas. India therefore reads the Commission as part of a wider pattern of China-Pakistan coordination close to its own northern frontiers.

Every world map is an attempt to show a curved surface on a flat sheet, and that task cannot be done without some loss. The Earth is not a perfect sphere, and its surface is curved in every direction. Cartographers therefore use map projections, which are systematic rules for transferring the globe onto a plane. No single flat map can keep every feature of the globe correct at the same time. Mapmakers must choose which properties to protect, such as the size of landmasses, the shapes of countries, the distances between places, or the directions between them. Some maps are made to guide travellers at sea, while others serve thematic and statistical purposes, such as showing population density. A projection that works well for one purpose may mislead when used for another. Over time, different projections have been developed, each built around a different choice of property. Readers should therefore check which property a map keeps accurate before drawing conclusions about the world from its outlines. The choice of projection is a practical decision rather than a search for one perfect map. Understanding these trade-offs helps students read maps with care, and this is why many different projections continue to exist side by side in atlases, classrooms and official publications.

Semiconductors have become central to modern life because they power automobiles, hospitals, defence systems, aircraft, telecom networks and a wide range of consumer goods. Modern chips can hold billions of transistors within very small areas, which makes them essential for high-performance computing, artificial intelligence and digital services. Semiconductors sit at the base of the global electronics industry, a very large economic sector. The COVID-19 pandemic showed how risky it is when chip production is concentrated in a few places, and many countries have since tried to build their own capabilities. India's response is a national programme that seeks to build a complete semiconductor ecosystem, covering design, fabrication, packaging, research and skilled manpower. Its purpose is to give the sector financial and infrastructure support, so that domestic companies can grow and compete. The government hopes this will make India a dependable partner in the global value chain, in line with the vision of self-reliance and manufacturing for the world. Several areas of the programme are meant to move forward together, so that progress in design, equipment, factories and people keeps pace with one another. This approach turns a broad national goal into a set of concrete steps that can be tracked over time.

The Unified Payments Interface has grown into a large digital payment network that handles billions of transactions every month. Running such a network requires continuous spending on technology, cybersecurity, fraud prevention, server capacity and customer support. Until now, merchants have not paid any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions, which helped small businesses and informal sectors adopt digital payments. As the network expands, however, planners must decide how its upkeep should be funded. The answer proposed in the new framework is a fee on certain merchant payments, while everyday low-value transactions remain free. Officials have stressed that small merchants and ordinary users should not face additional costs. The fee is therefore aimed at larger merchant payments rather than at the many small transactions that make up daily life. Such a structure lets the payment ecosystem generate revenue that supports its own operation. Policymakers have sought a balance between funding the network and protecting the people who use it every day. UPI works in real time and around the clock, connecting individuals and merchants across banks. Its wide use has made it an important part of commerce for individuals and merchants alike. Because so many people rely on it, any change to how the network is priced affects a very large number of users and businesses.

Financial and trade cooperation was among the most detailed areas of the 18th BRICS Summit, which India hosted in New Delhi in 2026. Member countries discussed how cross-border trade could be made less vulnerable to currency swings and to disruptions in global financial markets. A dedicated risk-focused initiative was also discussed, linked to large infrastructure projects across the Global South and to the geopolitical risks that such projects carry. Small enterprises received particular attention, since many of them need steady cash flow to run their operations and compete in international markets. Support for young companies also formed part of the discussions. On the tax and customs side, the summit focused on sharing knowledge between national tax authorities and on joint action against smuggling and illicit financial flows, while stressing that genuine trade should continue without unnecessary obstruction. The conversations also highlighted the role of new technologies and digital solutions for development. The overall message was that a more resilient financial architecture would help developing economies manage external shocks while keeping trade flowing.

Earth observation satellites help governments see what is happening on the ground without sending anyone to the site. Their usefulness depends on where they are placed in space, the rocket that lifts them and the sensors they carry. ISRO has added a new satellite to this list, known in the booklet as EOS-05 and also called GISAT-1A. The satellite was lifted into space by an indigenous heavy-lift rocket from an Indian launch centre, and the mission is treated as a test of the country's launch capability. The spacecraft is described as an advanced Earth observation satellite meant for continuous and high-frequency imagery. Such imagery supports disaster response, border watch and farm monitoring. As the booklet notes, the choice of orbit determines geographical coverage, image resolution, revisit time and the mission application. The same imagery can help plan emergency responses and track weather events. The sections that follow describe the satellite, the orbit it uses and the other missions that share its theme. Students preparing for competitive examinations should note that such questions usually test the specific numbers, stages and names attached to a mission, since these details are easy to confuse.

Financial markets are looking beyond conventional projects towards the health of the seas and rivers. A new category of debt instrument is emerging to pay for work that keeps marine and freshwater ecosystems usable and protected over the long term. India plans to join this market through a bond issued by a company that focuses on the maritime sector. The bond will be arranged by a bank's capital markets arm, which has been appointed as arranger. Governments elsewhere have already experimented with similar tools, so the idea is not entirely new.

Science also produced a headline this month. A technology company said that an advanced artificial intelligence model had produced a proposed solution to a long-standing puzzle about how fluids move. Such claims are checked with formal tools that test every step of an argument. The puzzle concerns the equations that describe the motion of water, air and honey, and it belongs to a small group of famous challenges that a mathematics institute has highlighted.

Those equations are not merely theoretical. Engineers rely on them when they design aircraft and automobiles, and scientists use them to predict weather and model currents in the ocean. Progress on the puzzle would therefore matter far beyond mathematics.

Yemen's civil war has moved through phases of fighting, negotiation and fragile truces. After the Houthis took over large parts of the north, a Saudi-led coalition joined the conflict to support the government that is recognised internationally. Renewed fighting caused civilian displacement and disrupted local supply lines. Negotiators from the warring parties then tried to find a way out of the fighting through a package of agreements. The Stockholm Agreement was one such deal, and it covered several issues, including the city of Hodeidah and its ports. Ceasefire terms for Hodeidah set out how armed forces would move away from the ports and how the ports would be run by local forces. The agreements were meant to reduce violence and open a path to a wider political settlement. Diplomats kept returning to the talks table, hoping that partial deals could be turned into lasting arrangements.

Trade measures linked to Russian energy purchases raise questions about how long they will last. A measure that has been passed by the legislature and signed into federal law carries greater legal permanence. American trade policy also relies on older statutes that give the government tools to respond to foreign practices. One of these allows the trade representative to examine unfair conduct by other countries. Another permits restrictions on imports when they are seen as a risk to national security. The government has also used tariffs on certain imported metals, and it has applied tariffs connected with goods produced through forced labour. For a country like India, such instruments matter because they change the cost of exports and make trade talks more complicated. Officials and businesses often watch these tools closely because a single measure can affect many sectors at once. Understanding the legal route behind each tariff helps explain why some measures last longer than others.

The boundary between India and China has never been fully settled, and disagreements over it have produced a long chain of confrontations. Two stretches of the frontier sit at the heart of the dispute. One lies in the high region of Aksai Chin, which the two sides understand differently, each relying on its own historical line. The other involves Arunachal Pradesh, which China describes as part of Tibet while India administers it as a full state. The line in that area was agreed at a convention attended by Tibet, China and British India, but China refused to accept it, arguing that Tibet could not conclude treaties. Armed encounters and standoffs have since erupted in several places, including mountain passes in Sikkim and Arunachal and the plateau where three countries meet. A practical dividing line emerged after the war of the early 1960s, and both sides have since tried to prevent escalation through talks and confidence-building measures. Local commanders meet at designated points to resolve friction on the ground, while senior commanders negotiate withdrawals when standoffs become serious. Yet incidents continue in the high mountains. Understanding these disputed lines is therefore essential for reading news about the border, since each claim carries a long history behind it.

India's push into semiconductors uses several kinds of government support rather than a single measure. Some tools are aimed at manufacturing, with financial incentives for companies that set up production within the country and attract large investments. Others are aimed at design, because a country that can design its own chips depends less on imported technology. Academic institutions and start-ups are part of this effort, as they need access to specialised resources, training facilities and design infrastructure. Research bodies are also building their own processors, including designs based on an open instruction architecture, which adds to domestic technical strength. Support for design firms is planned over a long stretch so that they can move from early development to full deployment. Diplomacy plays a role as well. India has signed a strategic technology agreement with a major economy to expand cooperation in research, business and defence industry. It has also joined a coalition of countries that wish to protect the supply of critical minerals, manufacturing capacity and digital infrastructure. Together these steps reflect an attempt to lower dependence on other countries and to become a dependable part of the global chip supply network, which matters greatly in a world where supply disruptions can hurt many industries at once.

Digital payments work best when small transactions stay cheap for everyone who uses them. Households send money to one another every day, and shopkeepers in local markets often accept payments through a QR code displayed at the counter. Small businesses need protection from additional payment processing costs. Policymakers have therefore tried to protect the smallest users while still asking larger participants to share the cost of running the network. The new approach separates payments into groups. Some payments remain free regardless of who sends or receives them, while others attract a charge only when they are large. Certain sectors that provide essential services are placed in a separate group, where a fixed charge per transaction applies rather than a percentage. Investments routed through mutual funds and securities are charged at a lower rate, because that rate is meant to encourage greater use of digital payments in formal financial markets. Several upper limits also protect users. A single ceiling prevents very large payments from carrying an unlimited fee, and small merchants who earn only modest amounts through QR codes each month are exempt from the charge altogether. Together, these rules aim to keep ordinary digital payments affordable while the payment infrastructure keeps growing.

The 18th BRICS Summit also produced outcomes in areas that touch everyday life, including farming, public health, transport and climate. Member countries discussed how to make food supplies steadier, particularly when global prices move sharply. A proposed commodity marketplace was among the ideas, intended to make trade in farm produce among member countries more predictable. Cooperation on seeds, plant material and farm inputs was also highlighted, along with a farmer-centred framework for sharing information. In health, the focus was on promoting active living and on building support for mental well-being through shared training. Innovation in medicine was another theme, with attention to developing solutions that could be deployed widely in developing regions. On transport and logistics, members agreed to share technical knowledge about building resilient supply systems. Climate concerns were reflected in discussions about cleaner fuels for aviation, urban infrastructure able to withstand extreme weather, and the protection of natural carbon sinks such as tropical forests. Culinary exchanges were also part of the summit, with regional produce showcased to delegates. Together, these outcomes reflected an effort to link economic cooperation with practical improvements in people's livelihoods.

The NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar satellite, called NISAR in short, is a partnership between two space agencies and is described as the first joint Earth-observation satellite of its kind between them. Conventional cameras depend on visible light, but radar works differently. A synthetic aperture radar sends microwave pulses toward the ground and builds images from the returning signals, so it can produce sharp pictures in darkness and through clouds. The satellite is meant to study changes in the solid Earth. Its images help track surface deformation, which is useful for understanding earthquakes, volcanic activity and landslides. The same data can also support monitoring of floods, biomass, deforestation, crop health and soil moisture. The booklet calls its radar technology among the finest synthetic aperture radar systems ever designed. Its large receiving antenna and wide imaging swath make it suitable for mapping large surface areas in three dimensions. Because the satellite can detect minute ground shifts, its data is used for tectonic and structural analysis.

September brought a mix of schemes, events and honours. The country marked International Literacy Day with a national festival that focused on adults who never learned to read. The programme is meant to build basic reading, writing and calculating skills among learners who have passed the age of school.

Water also featured in the news. A major conference on water management brought together experts, officials and delegates to discuss solutions that can withstand a changing climate. The event is a flagship initiative of a central government ministry, and it has been rebranded for the current year.

In cinema, the nation's highest honour is named after a pioneer of Indian films. The award recognises an individual's outstanding contribution to the growth and development of Indian cinema. A veteran actor from Karnataka was selected for the 2024 award and became the second Kannada actor to receive it.

Beauty pageants made headlines too. The Miss World contest crowned a new titleholder from the Dominican Republic at its latest edition, and the next edition has already been planned for a future year in another country. An Indian contestant secured a place among the top forty.

facts.title: Mukalla strike and UAE troop withdrawal
facts.summary: Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes on Mukalla Port in southern Yemen after a consignment from Fujairah in the UAE arrived there, which Riyadh alleged contained arms for separatist groups. The UAE rejected the allegation, saying the vehicles were meant exclusively for its own forces. The UAE then pulled its troops out, citing security risks, a counter-terrorism-only mandate and the view that Yemen's future should be decided by Yemenis.
facts: Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes on Mukalla Port in southern Yemen.
The strike followed the arrival of a consignment from Fujairah (UAE).
Riyadh alleged the consignment contained arms meant for southern separatist groups.
The UAE said the shipment consisted of vehicles meant exclusively for UAE forces.
The UAE termed the claims of an arms transfer to separatists unfounded.
Security concern: escalating airstrikes raised risks to UAE personnel in the region.
Limited mandate: the UAE's military presence in Yemen is confined to counter-terrorism operations.
Political messaging: Yemen's future political structure should be determined by Yemenis themselves.

facts.title: Appointment, Tenure and Removal of CEC and ECs
facts.summary: The CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 replaced the 1991 Act and provides for appointment by the President on the recommendation of a Selection Committee, following the Supreme Court's directive in Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India (2023). The CEC and ECs enjoy Supreme Court Judge-level salary and benefits. The CEC serves for six years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier, and is removed through the same process as a Supreme Court Judge.
facts: Anoop Baranwal vs Union of India (2023): five-judge bench directed appointment on the advice of a Selection Committee
Earlier, the President made appointments on the advice of the Prime Minister
The 2023 Act replaced the Election Commission (Conditions of Service of Election Commissioners and Transaction of Business) Act, 1991 on conditions of service and transaction of business
Selection Committee: Prime Minister, a Union Cabinet Minister, and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha
Search Committee, headed by the Minister of Law and Justice, proposes a panel of five names
Selection Committee can consider names beyond the shortlist and can function despite vacancies
Tenure: six years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier; not eligible for re-appointment
An EC appointed as CEC: combined term as EC and CEC must not exceed six years
CEC and ECs enjoy Supreme Court Judge-level salary and benefits
CEC is removed by the same process as a Supreme Court Judge

facts.title: NISAR: NASA-ISRO radar satellite
facts.summary: NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) is described as the first joint Earth-observation satellite of NASA and ISRO. As a radar satellite it uses microwave pulses to capture sharp images in darkness and through clouds, unlike cameras that rely on visible light. Its data supports study of solid Earth processes, natural hazards, biomass and crop health.
facts: First joint Earth-observation satellite by NASA and ISRO
Uses microwave pulses, so it works in darkness and through clouds
World's first radar satellite using dual S- and L-band frequencies
Designed for a 3-year mission life
Orbit: 747 km, Sun-Synchronous (Low Earth) Orbit with a 12-day repeat cycle
The NASA-side radar, with a wavelength of about 24 cm, was developed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL)
Sweep SAR captures wide 3D high-resolution images over a 242 km swath
Large 12-metre antenna for receiving signals
Detects minute ground shifts for tectonic and structural analysis
Tracks biomass, deforestation, crop health and soil moisture; assesses earthquakes, floods, landslides and volcanoes

facts.title: International Conventions and Diplomacy
facts.summary: The European Commission President has proposed exploring an 'Associate Member' relationship that could let Canada take part more closely in selected EU frameworks without full membership. Under the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, 128 countries reached a consensus on a working definition of lethal autonomous weapons systems. CITES regulates international trade in endangered wild species through three appendices, and the Montreal Protocol governs the phase-out of ozone-depleting substances and the Kigali Amendment mandates the phase-down of hydrofluorocarbons.
facts: EU proposal to explore an 'Associate Member' relationship, illustrated with Canada
'Associate Membership' is not an established membership category under the EU's foundational treaties
Treaty revision would require all 27 EU Member States to agree
Association Agreement under Article 217 of the TFEU is a more flexible alternative
Association Agreement needs unanimous approval in the Council and the consent of the European Parliament
CCW adopted in 1980 and entered into force in 1983
128 countries reached consensus on a working definition of Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS)
CITES has 185 Parties; India became a Party in 1976
CITES species are listed in three appendices by conservation status and trade sensitivity
Montreal Protocol (1987) led to a 99% phase-out of controlled ozone-depleting substances; Kigali Amendment (2016) mandates phase-down of HFCs

facts.title: Science, Environment and Culture
facts.summary: PRATUSH is a proposed Indian mission, while CosmoCube is a proposed lunar-orbiting mission led by scientists associated with the Royal Astronomical Society and University of Cambridge, both aimed at detecting the 21-cm signal from the early universe, while NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has been launched to study dark energy and exoplanets. Five young orangutans rescued in Odisha were moved to a zoo, and orangutans are native only to Borneo and Sumatra. World Rhino Day on 22 September highlighted the five rhino species, and the 2024 National Film Awards were announced.
facts: CosmoCube: proposed lunar-orbiting satellite to detect the 21-cm radio signal from the early universe
PRATUSH: Probing ReionizATion of the Universe using Signal from Hydrogen, by the Raman Research Institute with ISRO
Cosmic Dark Ages lie between about 380,000 years and about 200 million years after the Big Bang
Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy and operates near Sun-Earth L2
Five young orangutans rescued in Balasore (Odisha) and moved to Nandankanan Zoological Park
Orangutans are not native to India; their natural range is the tropical forests of Borneo and Sumatra
World Rhino Day is observed on 22 September; the 2026 theme is 'Keep the Five Alive'
Greater One-Horned Rhino is the largest of the five rhino species and is concentrated in Kaziranga National Park, Assam
National Film Awards were established in 1954 and have been administered by the Directorate of Film Festivals since 1973
Best Feature Film award went to Article 370 (Hindi)

facts.title: Upper Bhadra Project and Bhadra River
facts.summary: A trial run of the Upper Bhadra Project carried water from the Bhadra Reservoir to Gonur Lake in Chitradurga district through the Chitradurga Branch Canal. The development marks the start of the project's operational phase and meets a long-standing demand for reliable water in parts of central Karnataka. The project is the first irrigation project in Karnataka to receive National Project Status from the Union Government. The Bhadra river rises in the Western Ghats and eventually becomes part of the Krishna river system.
facts: Trial run carried water from Bhadra Reservoir to Gonur Lake, Chitradurga district
Route used: Chitradurga Branch Canal
Marks the beginning of the project's operational phase
Fulfils a long-standing demand for reliable water in parts of central Karnataka
Karnataka irrigation project to receive National Project Status from the Union Government
Bhadra River originates in the Western Ghats, near Gangamoola Peak
Bhadra joins Tunga River at Koodli, near Shivamogga
The confluence gives rise to the Tungabhadra River, a tributary of the Krishna River
Krishna river system ultimately drains into the Bay of Bengal
